messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Harjit Singh is an 80-year-old widowed Coast Guard veteran who still works in a reduced civilian support role near the harbor, and he dates the beginning of his trouble to an accident several years ago during a shoreline rescue exercise in a wooded coastal area. A younger crewman was moving equipment down a steep, brush-covered embankment while Harjit directed the team. There had been sirens from emergency vehicles on the access road above, gulls, surf, and shouted orders crossing over each other. Harjit gave a command too quickly, and the crewman lost his footing, tumbling onto rocks below and sustaining devastating injuries. Harjit remembers seeing the man’s body twisted among wet branches and hearing the sirens continue as if nothing had happened. Ever since, natural settings resembling that stretch of coast—tree line, damp earth, salt air—have carried a terrible charge for him, and even routine talk about “next year” or retirement can land with the force of accusation, because the future is precisely what he feels he damaged for another man.

What stays with him is not a continuous memory but a broken set of pieces. When he tries to recall the event on purpose, he says his mind “goes blank where it matters,” yet at other times the whole scene returns with overpowering vividness: the smell of mud and seawater, the rising sirens, the sight of brush shaking where the man fell. Because these fragments arrive disconnected and then suddenly all at once, he has grown increasingly sensitive to cues around him. A siren on the street outside the station, a path through coastal scrub, even conversation about upcoming plans can pull the memory forward before he knows what is happening. He has come to dread those moments not only because they are distressing, but because they seem to prove to him that the event is still lodged in him in some dangerous, unfinished way.

Over time Harjit has come to believe the accident happened because of the kind of man he is. He does not describe himself as having made a mistake so much as being fundamentally flawed, “the sort of person who ruins things.” That belief has made him scan constantly for danger, as if letting down his guard would expose more of this defect. In unfamiliar places he becomes uneasy because he cannot quickly map exits, hazards, or where people are standing. At meetings he quietly chooses the seat that feels most protected, usually with a wall behind him and a clear line to the door. When he feels keyed up in this way, the world itself seems to fill with reminders: the wail of an ambulance becomes unbearable, and if someone at work starts discussing future staffing or long-term plans, he feels a jolt of shame, as though he has no right to imagine a future after costing someone else so much.

His response has been to fight his own mind. He tells himself the incident was not really as bad as he remembers, or that perhaps he has exaggerated its seriousness over the years. At other times he forces himself into bright, corrective thoughts—telling himself to focus only on blessings, to think positively, to stop dwelling. Most often he tries to push the images away the instant they begin. These efforts make sense to him because they are driven by a desperate wish not to be the kind of man he fears he is. Yet the more firmly he suppresses the scene or insists it was not real, the less coherent his memory becomes when he tries to approach it deliberately, and the more violently it seems to return through sirens, shoreline brush, or casual talk of the future. Afterward he is left feeling even more disturbed by himself, as if only a defective person would need to deny something so grave.

The cycle has tightened in his daily life. At the harbor he avoids unfamiliar assignments and dislikes going to new locations unless he has studied them in advance. Even on ordinary errands he scans for the safest chair in a diner or waiting room. He has also become more reckless in smaller, unsettling ways, taking physical risks he dismisses with a shrug, as though his own safety matters less than it used to. Those moments are followed by a grim self-recognition that deepens his self-blame. When he has spent a day on edge, his memory is more likely to break through in full sensory form that night; when that happens, he doubles down on pushing it out of mind the next day, which leaves him even more reactive to the next siren or stand of trees. Since his wife died, there is no one at home to interrupt this pattern, and his world has narrowed around routes and settings he feels he can control.

He finally sought help after freezing during a planning conversation at work about next season’s training schedule. Someone mentioned the future of the unit, a siren sounded outside, and he was abruptly back on that embankment, smelling wet earth and hearing his own command. He had to leave the room and later sat in his truck shaken and ashamed, convinced his mind was failing and that he was still dangerous to others. What he fears most is not simply remembering, but confirming his belief that there is something rotten in his character. What he hopes, though he says this cautiously, is to understand why the past still arrives as if it is happening now and whether he can live whatever years remain without bracing against every sound, every landscape, and every mention of what comes next.
